content: Genital warts are a common condition that, while typically harmless, can cause significant physical discomfort and psychological distress. Various treatment options are available, including the use of topical 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU). This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of 5-FU as a topical treatment for genital warts in individuals who are not immunocompromised. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, covering studies up to August 2009. There were no restrictions on language or publication type. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults aged 18 years or older. Comparisons included 5-FU versus placebo or no treatment, 5-FU versus other treatments (topical or systemic), and 5-FU combined with other treatments versus various other therapeutic approaches. Six trials involving a total of 988 participants (645 women and 343 men) were included in the analysis. These trials reported eight different treatment comparisons. Two studies mentioned participant withdrawals and dropouts, but none performed an intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis. The results indicated that 5-FU was more effective in achieving a cure compared to placebo or no treatment, with a relative risk (RR) of 0.39 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.23 to 0.67). When compared to meta-cresol-sulfonic acid (MCSA), 5-FU showed a relative risk of 2.11 (95% CI 0.83 to 5.37), and when compared to Podophyllin (2%, 4%, or 25%), the relative risk was 1.26 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.82). No statistically significant differences were observed in treatment failure rates when comparing 5-FU to CO2 laser therapy (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.11) or 5-FU combined with low-dose interferon alpha-2a (INFα-2a) (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.19). However, worse outcomes were noted for 5-FU alone compared to 5-FU combined with high-dose INFα-2a (RR 10.78, 95% CI 1.50 to 77.36) and 5-FU combined with CO2 laser therapy and high-dose INFα-2a (RR 7.97, 95% CI 2.87 to 22.13). The authors concluded that the included trials exhibited significant variability in methodology and quality, resulting in weak overall evidence. Cure rates varied across treatments, and while 5-FU demonstrated inferior results compared to combinations involving high-dose INFα-2a and CO2 laser therapy, it still showed therapeutic potential. The use of topical 5-FU should not be dismissed, but its benefits and risks remain unclear. Further high-quality studies are necessary to better define its role in the treatment of genital warts.
